one_line_reason: The one clean single-ingredient trial (positive antispastic effect) is in spinal spasticity patients, and the rest of the human evidence is old ALS trials combining L-threonine with pyridoxal phosphate in a clinical disease population.

selected.intervention: oral L-threonine 6 g/day, double-blind placebo-controlled crossover
selected.why_selected: The cleanest single-ingredient, dose-stated human RCT in the shortlist, with a stated 'modest but definite antispastic effect'

selected.population: patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (95 randomized, 77 completers)
selected.intervention: oral L-threonine 4 g/day plus pyridoxal phosphate 160 mg/day vs branched-chain amino acids vs placebo, 6 months
selected.primary_outcome: disease progression (muscle strength, isometric torque, forced vital capacity, weight, activities of daily living)
selected.why_selected: Long-running controlled ALS trial reporting greater weight loss and a substantially greater decline in forced vital capacity in the L-threonine group versus placebo, though threonine was combined with pyridoxal phosphate

selected.population: patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multicenter trial
selected.intervention: oral L-threonine plus pyridoxal-5-phosphate vs branched-chain amino acids vs placebo, 6 months
selected.dose_as_stated: not stated in this electrophysiology sub-analysis
selected.primary_outcome: electrophysiologic measures of lower motor neuron loss and reinnervation; primary clinical endpoint was muscle strength
selected.why_selected: Companion analysis from the same negative ALS drug trial as 8909433, included for completeness though it reports secondary electrophysiologic endpoints rather than direct efficacy

blockers: The two ALS trials (8909433, 11231032) dose L-threonine only in combination with pyridoxal phosphate/pyridoxal-5-phosphate, not as a standalone exposure
All three selected trials are in clinical neurological-disease populations (ALS, spinal spasticity) under medical supervision, not general supplement users

The trials are from 1993-2001, predating current reporting standards, and the underlying disease context (ALS, spasticity) is unrelated to why L-threonine is marketed as a general amino-acid supplement today

handoff_pmids.note: Randomized, graded-dose (0-12 g/day) safety and tolerability trial of L-threonine in healthy adults; reports biochemical/anthropometric safety parameters, not a health-outcome efficacy claim

excluded_pmids.reason: WITHDRAWN Cochrane review of amino acids (BCAA or L-threonine) for ALS; superseded/withdrawn version of 14583978
Cochrane review of amino acids (BCAA or L-threonine) for ALS; a review-level synthesis of the same primary trials already represented by 8909433 and 11231032, not additional primary data
Overview of Cochrane reviews of symptomatic treatments for ALS/MND generally; no L-threonine-specific efficacy data given in the retrieved abstract
Cochrane review of treatments for cramps in ALS/MND; no L-threonine-specific data given in the retrieved abstract
Tests a 5-amino-acid blend (leucine, threonine, lysine, isoleucine, valine) plus chromium picolinate for postprandial glucose; a combination product, not isolated L-threonine
Tests a protein supplement (Tonexis HP) plus L-threonine and L-methionine, combined with medroxyprogesterone acetate, in HIV-infected patients; combination product and clinical population
Tests an 8-amino-acid blend plus carbohydrates in older men; combination product, and found no significant difference from control on muscle strength/size
Metabolomics review of biomarkers in diabetic retinopathy; threonine appears only as a measured biomarker, not a supplementation intervention
